analysis.one_liner: Gives workers 10 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a birth, adoption, or a child's serious illness.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a Senate subcommittee: it drew no cosponsors, got no vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have entitled employees at companies with 50 or more workers to 10 weeks of leave, without pay, after a birth, adoption, foster placement, or a child's serious health condition, with the right to return to the same or an equivalent job. Employers would have had to keep health insurance in place during the leave and could not penalize workers for taking it. Federal civil service employees would have gotten the same rights. It was introduced by Senator DeConcini in May 1989, sent to a Senate subcommittee two weeks later, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees at employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act with 50 or more employees (dropping to 35 after three years) who have worked at least 12 months and 900 hours. They could take up to 10 workweeks of leave in any 24-month period for the birth or adoption of a child, a foster care placement, or to care for a child with a serious health condition, and return to their job or an equivalent one. Health coverage would continue during leave. Federal civil service employees would get parallel rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and caregivers at mid-size and larger employers

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 10 workweeks of parental leave during any 24-month period for birth, adoption or foster placement, or to care for a child with a serious health condition, with the right to be restored to the same or an equivalent position.

Requires employers to maintain group health plan coverage during the leave at the same level as if the employee had kept working, so a family does not lose insurance while a parent is home with a newborn or sick child.

Makes it unlawful for an employer to interfere with these rights or discriminate against someone for filing a charge or testifying, and lets the Labor Department or the employee enforce the rules in court, with attorneys' fees available to a prevailing party.
Extends the same parental leave entitlement to federal civil service employees, with job protection and continued health enrollment.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers bear the cost: they must hold jobs open or find equivalents, keep paying the employer share of health premiums during leave, handle certification and notice paperwork, and face damages and legal exposure for violations. The leave itself is unpaid, so wages during leave come from the employee's own savings or substituted vacation or personal leave.
analysis.who_pays_short: Covered employers of 50 or more workers

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid; an employee may substitute accrued vacation or personal leave, but a worker living paycheck to paycheck may be unable to afford taking any of the 10 weeks.

Employers with 50 or more employees face new compliance obligations — holding positions open, continuing health coverage, certification paperwork, and potential damages including liquidated damages up to triple lost compensation — and the threshold drops to 35 employees after three years, covering smaller firms.
The bill is largely redundant for workers whose employers already offer generous paid leave, since existing benefits that are more protective are preserved but nothing new is added for them.

Employers may require medical certification, second and even third opinions for leave tied to a child's health condition, and periodic status reports, which adds hurdles for families in stressful situations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For working parents, the upside is real: a legal right to take time off for a birth, adoption, or a sick child without losing the job or the family's health insurance. The main weakness is that the leave is unpaid, so it protects mostly those who can afford to go without a paycheck; a paid-leave or wage-replacement design would have reached more families. Employer costs are real but modest compared with later versions of this policy, and the bill was deliberately written to accommodate employers — notice rules, certification, small-business exemptions, and a required study of effects on firms under 50 employees.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee two weeks after introduction and sent to its subcommittee on children and families, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Dennis DeConcini introduced the Parental Leave Act of 1989 in the Senate on May 2, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.

On May 17, 1989, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Children, Family, Drugs, Alcohol, and the committee requested executive comments from the Department of Labor, the Office of Personnel Management, and the Office of Management and Budget.
No further action was recorded; the bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, committee markup, or floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The idea did not die permanently: Congress later enacted a closely related family and medical leave law, which President Clinton signed in 1993 after similar bills passed in the early 1990s.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have been covered by the mandate came out ahead in the short run — no new leave obligations, no health-coverage costs during leave, no litigation exposure. Working parents gained nothing from this bill, though the same policy eventually became law in 1993.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Covered employers avoided a new leave mandate

for.name: Sen. Dennis DeConcini
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Parental Leave Act of 1989 and served as its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to its subcommittee on children and families, and never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: Edward M. Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no further action on the bill after referring it to a subcommittee; it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandated parental leave bills of this era on cost and burden grounds as Congress debated the proposal through the late 1980s and early 1990s.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows no party-line split; the sponsor was a Democrat and the bill died quietly in a Democratic-controlled Senate committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to hold jobs open for parents on leave, keep paying health premiums during leave, and face damages for violations. Those costs are the flip side of the job security the bill gives workers.
Title II would have required federal agencies to grant the same 10-week parental leave to civil service employees, an added personnel cost borne by taxpayers as employer.

They would have been exempt at first, and only brought in at the 35-employee level after three years, while a mandated study examined effects on firms under 50 — leaving them free of the new obligations their larger competitors would bear.
